sense_notes: Speaker witnessed it. Mandatory slot; scopes over negation (D30).
Speaker was told it. Source is someone else's statement.
Speaker reasoned it out from evidence, did not witness it.
Known without a source: definition, convention, common knowledge.
Speaker is committed to doing it. The commitment half of English 'will' (D31).
Speaker expects it, without commitment. The prediction half of English 'will'.
Offered for testing or discussion, not claimed. A hypothesis, never a finding (D34).
Speaker relies on it as an assumption; the thing being built on.
Speaker knows it may go wrong and says so.
Speaker insists, against pushback. Carries emphasis (D32).
Before now. Present is unmarked.
After now, strictly temporal; intention and prediction are stance (D31).
Piece of the verb ending, before tense. Evidential scopes over it (D32).
Last piece of the embedded verb's ending; makes a clause a complement or a relative clause (D33).
On the argument acted on. Subject is bare.
On the argument that is a place, source or goal of location.
On the possessor, which precedes the possessed.
Sentence-final. The answer supplies the evidential (D30, D33).
Speaker. Takes case markers, nothing else.
Addressee.
Near or just mentioned; person or thing. No gender, no animacy.
Far or earlier mentioned; person or thing.
Accompaniment or instrument. Separate word after its argument.
Beneficiary or purpose.
Origin, cause or source, when the location case is not enough.
Knowing carve, side 1 of 3: known because it was tried or observed to hold. Not by definition (side 2), not belief (side 3). As an argument: a tested fact.
Knowing carve, side 2 of 3: known because that is what the word, rule or convention says. Not tested, not believed. As an argument: a definition, a convention.
Knowing carve, side 3 of 3: held to be so without test or definition. Covers English believe, assume, take for granted. As an argument: a belief.
Error carve, side 1 of 3: a wrong act by someone. The person erred. Not the fault it may have left in the thing (side 2), not what happened at run time (side 3).
Error carve, side 2 of 3: a wrong state in the thing itself, present whether or not anything has gone wrong yet. English bug, defect. Verbal: to be faulty.
Error carve, side 3 of 3: something went wrong when it ran or was used. The event, not its cause. English crash, fail, error at run time. Verbal: to fail.
Asking carve, side 1 of 3: a request to be told something. Same consonant family as the question particle. Not a request for action (side 2), not a check (side 3).
Asking carve, side 2 of 3: a request that someone do something. English please, could you, request. Never a question about facts.
Asking carve, side 3 of 3: asking whether something taken as so actually holds. English confirm, verify with someone, sanity-check. The answer is a stance or evidential.
Change carve, side 1 of 3: change what is broken so that it works. Presupposes a fault or failure. Not alter (side 2), not build (side 3).
Change carve, side 2 of 3: change what already works into something else that works. English modify, update, refactor, tweak. Nothing was broken.
Change carve, side 3 of 3: bring into existence what was not there. English make, create, write from scratch, implement. As an argument: a thing built.

Lumped root (D35): the act of doing something in order to observe what happens. One root for lab experiment, unit test, and trying a thing to see. The evidential carries the result. As an argument: a test, an experiment, an attempt.

The one interrogative root. Bare: what. Before a root as a determiner: which (D44). With location case: where. With 'for': why. With 'with': how, by what means. With the time root: when. With the person root: who. There are no other question words.
A human. Verbal use: to be a person, to be someone. With the interrogative before it: who.
Make something go: execute a program, start a process, operate a machine. Not moving on foot; that is not in the language yet.
Take in what is written or displayed. As an argument: a reading, a read.
Put down in writing or in code. As an argument: a piece of writing, code written.
Direct attention at; examine, inspect. Does not imply finding anything. As an argument: a look, an inspection.
Locate or discover what was looked for or not. Implies success. As an argument: a finding.
Any entity, abstract or concrete. The default noun; use a narrower root when one exists.
What brings something about. Verbal use: to cause. Paired with result.
What is brought about; an outcome, output, the value a test gives. Verbal use: to result, to come out as.
A point or stretch of time. With the interrogative before it: when. Verbal use: to take time, to last.
Identifier of a thing or person: a name, a label, a variable name. Verbal use: to name, to call.
A document or file on a machine; also a page of text. Verbal use: to file, to save as a file.
Set two or more things side by side to see how they differ or agree. As an argument: a comparison.
Find how much or how big by a procedure with a unit. As an argument: a measurement, a measure.
Let time pass until something happens. As an argument: a wait, a delay.
A component of a larger thing. Verbal use: to be part of.
One root: nominal use is a number or quantity, verbal use is to count. English splits these; the language does not (D25).
A location, physical or in a file or system. With the interrogative before it: where. Verbal use: to be located at, to put.
A computer, device or mechanism that runs. Verbal use: to be mechanical, to run automatically.
Large in size, amount or importance. Stative: 'the file bigs' = the file is big. Small is its own root, not big-NEG.
Little in size, amount or importance. Own root; not-big is weaker than small.
Good for its purpose; working well; approved of. Stative. As an argument: a good, a benefit.
Bad for its purpose; working badly; disapproved of. Own root; not-good is weaker than bad.
Identical or equivalent to the thing compared with ('with'). Different = same-NEG; there is no separate root (D25).
Is the case; holds. False = true-NEG; there is no separate root (D25). As an argument: a truth, a fact that holds.
Finished, complete. Stative. Not-done = still in progress. Broken is not a root: use fault verbally (D35).
Earlier than its argument, in time or in order. After its argument like the other relational words. 'this time before' = before now.
Later than its argument, in time or in order. 'test after' = after the test.
Numeral 1. Numerals stand before the root they count, like determiners (D44, D48).
Numeral 2.
Numeral 3.
Numeral 4.
Numeral 5. Base of 6-9: five-one, five-two, five-three, five-four, written solid.
Numeral 10. A numeral before ten multiplies it, anything after adds: two-ten = 20, ten-five = 15, two-ten-five-one = 26.
5+1, written solid. Composed, but listed so the corpus can count it.
5+2, written solid.
5+3, written solid.
5+4, written solid.

Arrange the pieces of an experiment or benchmark so that it can run: the apparatus, the configuration, the harness. As an argument: the setup, the configuration. Sits outside the change carve: it is neither fix, alter nor build; it is placing what already exists into working order for a run. Not the test itself (the lumped experiment root covers that).

A part taken to stand for a whole: a specimen, a data point, a subset drawn from a population. Verbal: to sample, to draw a subset. Not the whole body of data (data root), not a part in the structural sense (the part root).

What is deliberately kept unchanged so that a comparison is fair: the control group, the baseline run, the fixed condition. Verbal: to hold fixed, to keep constant. Paired with the vary root. Not fix in the repair sense (that is the change carve).

What is deliberately set to different values across runs: the independent variable, the factor being changed. Verbal: to vary, to set to a different value on purpose. Outside the change carve: nothing is repaired, modified or built; a value is chosen. Paired with the control root. Unplanned change is not this root: use increase or decrease, or same-NEG.

The standard a measurement counts in: seconds, bytes, runs. As a determiner-free nominal beside a number. Verbal: to be the unit of, to be counted in. Not the number itself (number root), not the measuring act (measure root).

A greater amount, much, many. Stative: the count is more, there is more of it. An amount word, not a grammatical comparison: the language has no 'more than X' construction. Own root; less is not more-NEG.
A smaller amount, little, few. Stative: the count is less, there is less of it. Own root; not-more is a weaker claim than less. An amount word, not a comparison.

Go up in amount over time; grow, rise. The change event, not the state (the state is the more root). As an argument: an increase, a rise. Undirected or unplanned change; deliberate setting of a value is the vary root. Outside the change carve.
Go down in amount over time; shrink, drop, fall. Own root, not increase-NEG (not-increasing includes staying flat). As an argument: a decrease, a drop. Paired with increase.

Do the same thing again: rerun, iterate, loop, try again. One root for the loop in code, the repeat of an experiment, and the adverb again (the activity done again is its object, or it stands alone). As an argument: a repetition, a run, a trial, an iteration, a loop.

Put an observed value or event into a durable store: log it, write it into a table or a file. As an argument: a record, a log entry. Carved from write (producing text or code) and from data (the body of records); this root is the capturing act and one captured item.

Attend to what happens and take it in: watch, notice, perceive during a run. As an argument: an observation. Carved from look (aim attention at a thing; may see nothing) and find (locate what was sought; implies success): observe is seeing what occurs, the ground of the direct evidential.

The body of recorded values from a run or a set of runs: dataset, measurements taken together. Verbal: to be the data of, to serve as data for. Carved from record (one entry or the act of logging) and sample (a subset drawn from it).

A regularity across data: a trend, a recurring shape, a correlation. Verbal: to follow a pattern, to recur regularly. Carved against chance: a pattern is what is not chance, and it does not by itself say what the cause is.
What happens with no cause in the variable: randomness, noise, luck, coincidence. Verbal: to happen by chance. Carved against cause and against pattern; 'from chance' names the null explanation.

How far a set of values differ among themselves: variance, scatter, noise band, range. Stative: the results are spread out. As an argument: the spread. Not same-NEG (which is about two things differing), not the pattern.
The typical or central value of a set: mean, median, the middle. Verbal: to average, to take the mean of. As an argument: the average.
A bound a value must not pass: a threshold, a cap, a timeout, a maximum or minimum. Verbal: to limit, to bound, to cap. Not big or small (which are about size, not about a bound).

A named piece of code that takes input and gives a result; a procedure, routine, method. Verbal: to act as a function, to compute. Calling a function is run + function (no separate call root). Sits beside part (a component of anything) and write-as-argument (code in general): a function is the unit of code that runs on its own.

What a name, slot or expression holds or evaluates to; the content, not the container. Verbal: to be worth, to evaluate to. Carved against result (what a run brings about; the output) and against variable (the slot that holds a value). A number and a text are kinds of value.

A named slot that holds a value; a variable, a field, a store. Verbal: to store, to assign, to put a value into a slot. Same consonant family as value: variable is the container, value the content. Not name (the label of the slot; that is the name root) and not place (a location).

What is fed into a function, test or machine before it runs: an argument, a parameter, input data. Verbal: to feed in, to give as input. Paired with result, which already covers output; there is no separate output root.

A yes/no test inside a run that selects which path runs next; a branch, an if-condition, a branch point in code. Verbal: to choose, to branch on, to select. Lumped: condition and choice are one root, the choosing thing and the choosing act. Not the test root (doing something to observe), not check-an-assumption (asking a person). A person choosing is the choose root.

One line of a file or of code; a row. Verbal: to be on a line, to line up. Counts with numerals: ten lines. Not part (any component) and not place (a location), though a line can be named as a place with the location case.

Halt a running thing or come to an end; a stop, a halt, the end of something. Verbal: to stop, to halt, to end. Lumped: stop, halt, end, terminate are one root. Opposite of run (make go) and of begin (same consonant family). Not done (finished, complete): a thing can stop without being done. Transitive (stop the test) or intransitive (the test stopped). Stopped is not done: stop is the cease event, done (w0065) is completion.

Come into motion or be the first point of a stretch; a beginning, a start, the head of a file. Verbal: to begin, to start. Same consonant family as stop. Not the run root: run makes a thing go, begin marks the first point of anything, a run, a test, a file, a stretch of time. Transitive (begin the test) or intransitive (the test began).

The state of a thing as of one point in time, kept so it can be gone back to; a version, a revision, a snapshot, a commit. Verbal: to save as a version, to commit. Not copy (a duplicate that exists alongside) and not alter (the change itself).
A message: words or output sent from one party to another, what a machine prints when it fails, a notice. Verbal: to output a message. The act of a person saying or telling is the say/tell root.

Look at someone's work and give a verdict of good or bad; a review, a judgement, a verdict. Verbal: to review, to judge, to evaluate. Carved against look (inspect, no verdict implied), against check-an-assumption (asking whether something taken as so holds) and against compare (side by side, no verdict). Approve and reject are review + good / review + bad.

A category that things fall into; a kind, a type, a class, a sort. Verbal: to be of a kind, to be a type of. Used for the type of a value (number, text) and for kinds of anything. Not same (identical): two things of one kind are not the same thing.

Many things in a sequence; a list, a sequence, an ordering. Verbal: to list, to order, to sort, to put in sequence. Lumped: list and ordering are one root. Not number/count (how many) and not part (one member); a member of a list is part + possessor.

A duplicate made from an original and existing alongside it; a copy, a clone. Verbal: to copy, to duplicate. Not version (a saved state of the same thing over time) and not build (a new thing from nothing) or same (identical: a copy is same-with the original, but is a second thing).

Take a thing out so that it is no longer there; a removal, a deletion. Verbal: to remove, to delete, to drop. Outside the change carve: fix, alter and build all leave a thing present; remove ends its presence. Not stop (halts a run; the thing remains).

Move a thing from one holder to another; a giving, a handing-over, a passing of a value to a function. Verbal: to give, to pass, to send, to hand. The receiver takes the location case as goal. Lumped: give, pass, send, hand over are one root. Not message (words sent) and not find-from (get).

Recently built, changed or arrived; fresh. Stative: 'the version news' = the version is new. Old = new-NEG; there is no separate root, following the same/true pattern (D25). Before a root as an attributive stative, like big and small.

Make visible or evident: display, print to a screen, demonstrate, point out to someone. The thing shown is the object; the person shown takes the location case as recipient (D57). As an argument: a display, a demonstration.

A sequence of characters as a value; a string, a word, a piece of text as data. Verbal: to be text, to be a string. Sits beside number as a kind of value. Not write (the act of writing, or code written) and not file (a document holding text) and not name (a label; a name is text, but not every text names).

Accept another person's claim or proposal; be of one mind with them. The other party takes 'with'; the claim agreed to is the object. Covers agree, accept, go along with. Not the trust stance (which is relying on something as an assumption) and not knowing by belief. Disagreeing as mere non-acceptance is agree-NEG; pushing back is its own root (object). As an argument: an agreement.

Speak against a claim or proposal; resist it in discussion. Stronger than agree-NEG, which only withholds acceptance. The claim pushed against is the object. Covers object, disagree, contest, push back. It is the pushback that the assert stance answers; assert is a stance on one's own claim, this root is an act against another's. As an argument: an objection.

Give an account of something so that the other person grasps it. The thing explained is the object; the hearer takes 'for'. Covers explain, account for, lay out, walk through. Not the reason itself (own root) and not saying in general (own root). As an argument: an explanation.

A reason as something a person offers: grounds, justification, the why given in argument. Carved from cause (w0047): cause is what actually brings a thing about in the world; reason is what someone puts forward as grounds, which may or may not be the cause. Verbal use: to give grounds for, to justify. With 'for' after the interrogative the question word for why stays as it is; this root is the answer to it.

Grasp what something means or how it works; follow an explanation. Not a side of the knowing carve: knowing is about a fact being held to hold, understanding is about the meaning or workings being grasped. Not understanding is understand-NEG; there is no separate root for confusion. As an argument: an understanding.

Hold in mind or bring back to mind something from before. The thing remembered is the object. Forgetting is lumped as remember-NEG: 'I forgot the name' is 'I do not remember the name'; 'do not forget X' is an imperative of remember. Not knowing by test (w0026): that is about how the fact is warranted, this is about keeping it. As an argument: a memory of something.

The act of uttering something to someone. One root for say and tell. The addressee takes the location case, like every recipient (D57); the content is the object, or a subordinate clause. Corrected from the entry's original note, which said the addressee was the object (D67).

Respond to an ask of any of the three kinds (w0032-w0034). The person answered is the object; the content is a bare subordinate clause. Shares its second syllable with the asking family so that ask and answer are one audible pair. Not say in general (own root). As an argument: an answer, a reply.

Signify; stand for; be what a speaker intends by a word or act. Subject is the sign or the speaker, object is what is meant. Covers 'what does this mean' and 'I meant this'. Not name (w0050, the label itself) and not the intend stance (commitment to act). As an argument: a meaning.

Stative: plain, unambiguous, easy to grasp; said of an explanation, a reason, a name, a result. Unclear, vague and confusing are lumped as clear-NEG. Before another root it restricts it like the other statives (a clear name). Not true (w0064): a claim can be clear and false. As an argument: clarity.

Make someone's task easier or possible; assist. The person helped is the object; the task takes 'with'. A thing can be the subject ('the explanation helped'). Not fix (w0035) and not good (w0061). As an argument: help, assistance.

Settle an open question so that it is closed and acted on. The matter settled is the object. Carved from choose: deciding closes a question, choosing takes one item out of a set; one can decide without a set of alternatives and choose without closing anything. As an argument: a decision, as in the project's decisions file.

Take one item out of a set of alternatives. The item taken is the object; the set takes 'from'. Carved from decide (see that root). Shares its first syllable with the interrogative so that which-question and choice are audibly related. As an argument: a choice, the thing chosen.

Stative of a person (or a claim they made): correct about a matter. The matter takes the object case ('right about the cause'). Carved from true (w0064), which is about a proposition holding, and from mistake (w0029), which is a wrong act: being wrong is a state of the person's view. Wrong is lumped as right-NEG. Shares its first syllable with true.

Withhold belief from a claim; hold it in question. An act or state of the doubter, with the claim as object or as a bare subordinate clause. Carved from check (w0034), which is asking someone whether an assumption holds; doubt is internal and asks no one. Not belief-NEG (w0028): one can neither believe nor doubt. Shares its first syllable with check. As an argument: a doubt.

Talk something over together; the exchange itself. The matter is the object; the other party takes 'with'. Built audibly from person plus ask. Covers discuss, talk about, go over. Not ask (one-directional) and not say. As an argument: a discussion.

Alternative. Stands between the two things joined: two arguments, two predicates, or two clauses. In a question, asks which alternative holds. 'And' has no word: clauses are juxtaposed, arguments are joined with 'with' (D59).

Contrast between two clauses; stands between them. Not needed for mild contrast, which juxtaposition and stance already carry; used when the second clause runs against the expectation set by the first (D59).

Marks the clause before it as a condition. Follows its clause, like every other relational word (with, for, from, before, after), and sits in the same consonant family as them. The condition clause comes first and its predicate carries the general evidential, since a condition is stated as a rule, not as something witnessed; the main clause carries whatever evidential and stance it needs. No word for 'then' (D60).

The subject has what it takes to do the thing: a person is able, a machine or a value has the capacity, a state of affairs is within reach. Takes a subordinate clause as its complement, whose predicate carries the general evidential because the thing is not (yet) actual. Cannot = this root negated. Carved against the risk stance, which warns that something might go wrong: capacity is a fact about the subject, risk is the speaker's attitude to their own claim. Does not cover permission (D61).

Determiner standing before the root it quantifies, like a numeral (D44, D48): every test, all parts. With the thing root it is everything; with the person root, everyone. English needs every, all, everything, everyone and everybody; this is one word plus the roots that already exist (D62).

Negative determiner before the root it quantifies: no fault, no machine. The predicate is NOT also negated; the determiner alone carries the negation. With the thing root it is nothing; with the person root, nobody. Distinct from negating a predicate about a particular thing, which is still the negation affix (D62).

The subject wants the thing in the complement clause to be so. Modal root taking a subordinate clause whose predicate carries the general evidential (D61 irrealis rule); shares its first syllable with the other modal roots (able, should, allow), so the class is audible. Carved against the intend stance, which is commitment to act: wanting is not yet committing, and one can want what one cannot do.

The thing in the complement clause is what ought to be done or ought to hold. Obligation or advice, whoever the subject is. Carved against the intend stance (the speaker's own commitment) and against want (desire): should is a claim about what is right to do, not about the speaker's will. Modal root over a subordinate clause.

The subject is permitted the thing in the complement clause; someone or some rule permits it. Carved against the ability root: capacity is what the subject can do, permission is what the subject is let do. Negated it is 'must not'. Modal root over a subordinate clause.

Quick; takes little time; covers high speed of a machine, a run, a person acting. Stative ('the run fasts' = the run is fast) and the property named as an argument (speed as shortness of time). Own root; slow is its own root, not fast-NEG, on the big/small and good/bad pattern (D25 keeps negation only where it is genuinely the whole of the other sense). Carved from the time root (w0049, how long something lasts): fast is the rate, not the duration, and from more/less, which are amounts.

Takes much time; low speed. Own root, paired with fast: not-fast is a weaker claim than slow. Same first syllable as fast, differing vowel, so the pair is audible. Not the wait root (w0054, letting time pass until something happens): slow is a property of how a thing proceeds, waiting is an act.

The general root for performing any action: do, act, carry out, perform. Stands where no narrower root applies ('what did you do', 'nobody acted', 'do it now'), and takes as object the thing done. Deliberately the widest root in the language: build, fix, run, write and the rest are all narrowings of it, and the narrow root is preferred whenever one fits. As an argument: an act, an action, a deed. Not cause (w0047, what brings a thing about) and not work-as-a-thing-produced.

Close in space or in order; a short distance away. Stative ('the machine nears' = the machine is near) and, before a root or after a possessor, the region close to it ('the machine's near' = the vicinity of the machine), which takes the location case for 'near the machine'. Own root, paired with far. Not the place root (w0057, a location itself) and not before/after (w0066-w0067, which are about time and order).

A long distance away in space or in order. Stative, and as a region-nominal with the location case like near. Own root; not-near is weaker. Distance as a measured quantity is this root or its pair with the measure root; there is no separate root for distance.

The interior of a thing, and being in it: in, within, the inside. As an argument with the possessor and the location case: 'the file's inside at' = inside the file. Stative: 'it insides' = it is inside. Entering is the move root plus this with the location case; there is no separate root for enter. Carved from place (w0057, any location) and part (w0055, a component): a thing's inside is a region, not one of its pieces.

The exterior of a thing, and being out of it: out, outside, beyond it. Same shape of use as inside, with which it pairs: possessor plus location case for 'outside the machine'. Leaving is the move root plus this with the location case. Own root, not inside-NEG.

The region above a thing, and being higher than it: up, above, over, the top. With the location case for 'above it' and as the goal of the move root for 'move it up'. Spatial only: a value going up in amount is the increase root (w0085), never this. Own root, paired with down.
The region below a thing, and being lower than it: down, below, under, the bottom. Spatial only; a value going down in amount is the decrease root (w0086). Paired with up, sharing its first syllable.

Not shut: a state in which a thing can be entered, read from or written to, and the act of putting it into that state. One root for the act and the state, like the other physical-state roots; the evidential and tense carry the rest. Covers opening a file, a machine's cover, a way in. Not begin (w0103, the first point of a stretch): a thing can be open long before anything begins.

Shut: a state in which a thing cannot be entered or used, and the act of putting it into that state. Own root, paired with open and sharing its first syllable; not-open is a weaker claim than closed. Not stop (w0102, halting a run) and not done (w0065, finished).

Holding as much as it can, or as much as it is meant to hold: full, filled, at capacity. Stative, said of a file, a store, a machine, a list. Carved against more (w0083, a greater amount) and against the limit root (w0095, a bound a value must not pass): full is the state of having reached what the thing holds.

Holding nothing: empty, blank, vacant. Own root, paired with full; not-full includes everything in between and so will not serve. Said of a file, a store, a list, a place. Not none (w0136, the negative determiner) and not the removal act (w0110).

Takes much effort or skill to do; hard to carry out. Stative of a task, an act or a thing to be done. Own root, paired with easy. Carved against clear (w0124, plain and easy to grasp, which is about understanding) and against bad (w0062): a difficult task can be a good one. As an argument: difficulty.

Takes little effort or skill. Own root, paired with difficult and sharing its first syllable; not-difficult is a weaker claim. Not clear (w0124), which is about an explanation or a name being unambiguous, and not help (w0125), which is the act of making a task easier.

Much weight; hard to lift or move. Stative, and by extension of a load on a machine. Own root, paired with light-in-weight. Carved from big (w0059, size or importance): a small thing can be heavy. As an argument: weight in the sense of how heavy a thing is; measuring it is this root with the measure root (w0053).

Little weight; easy to lift or move. Own root, paired with heavy and sharing its first syllable. Weight only: light in the sense of illumination is not in the language, and light in the sense of easy is the easy root.

High in temperature: hot, warm. Stative, said of a machine, a place, a thing. Own root, paired with cold. Temperature only: there is no figurative sense. As an argument: heat, or temperature named through this root.
Low in temperature: cold, cool. Own root, paired with hot and sharing its first syllable; not-hot is a weaker claim than cold.

Come to hold a thing by one's own action: pick it up, get it, take it. The thing taken is the object; the source takes the from word or the location case. Carved from receive (its pair): taking is initiated by the taker, receiving by the giver. Not give (w0111, which moves a thing to another holder) and not find (w0045, locating what was sought).

Come to hold a thing because someone or something passed it: receive, get, be given, take delivery. The converse of the give root (w0111), which had no converse; the giver takes the from word. Carved from take (its pair, sharing its first syllable): the receiver does not initiate. Also used of a machine receiving input.

Keep a thing in hand or in place; grip it, hold on to it, keep hold of it. The physical act and the state of keeping something held. Carved from the true/hold root (w0064), which carries existence and possession in this language: that root says a thing is there or is someone's, this one says a hand or a mechanism is gripping it. Also the control root (w0080) is different again: that is keeping a value unchanged for a fair comparison.

Change place: move, shift, go, carry to another place. Transitive (move the part) or intransitive (the part moved). The goal takes the location case, the source the from word. Carved from run (w0041, making a thing go or execute, which need not change its place) and from give (w0111, which changes who holds a thing, not where it is).

Put two or more things together so that they hold as one: join, attach, connect, combine, merge. The things joined are the object, or one is the object and the other takes the with word. Paired with separate. Not build (w0037, bringing into existence what was not there) and not same (w0063): joined things stay two things.

Take apart what was together: separate, detach, split, take off. The thing separated is the object; what it is separated from takes the from word. Own root, not join-NEG, because it is an act and not the withholding of one. Not remove (w0110, which ends a thing's presence altogether).

All of a thing with none of it left out: the whole, the entirety, entire. Before a root it restricts it like the statives: the whole file, the entire machine. Carved from part (w0055, one component) as its counterpart, from every/all (w0135, which quantifies over many things, where this is about one thing complete), and from done (w0065, which is about a process finished).

The light stretch between two nights, and by extension one whole light-dark cycle when counted with a numeral (three days). Lumped deliberately: daytime and the counted cycle are one root, as in many languages; the dark stretch is its own root (night). Verbal use: to be day, for day to come. Not the general time root (a point or stretch of any size): this is the cycle the sky gives. Not a unit word: the unit root plus this root names it as a unit of measure.

The dark stretch between two days. Shares its first syllable with day so the pair is audible; it is not day-NEG, because the counted-cycle sense of day includes the night. Verbal use: to be night. A stretch, so it takes the location case for 'at night'.

Stative: at a point before the expected, due or proper one. Paired with late, which is its own root, not this one negated (not-early includes on time). Carved from the before relational word (w0066), which is purely relative to a named argument and says nothing about an expectation: early needs no argument, the expectation is understood. Before another root it restricts it like the other statives: an early stage, an early stop. As an argument: earliness.

Stative: at a point after the expected, due or proper one; overdue, delayed, behind. Shares its second syllable with early. Not the after relational word (w0067), which is relative to a named argument only. Where a deadline is actually named, 'after the time limit' says the same thing compositionally; this root is for when the due point is understood rather than stated. Not wait (w0054), which is letting time pass on purpose.

Stative of an event or a kind of event: it occurs at many points over a stretch of time. 'The failure oftens' = it fails often. Before a root it restricts it: frequent failure. Carved from the more root (w0083), which is amount, not rate, and from the numeral-plus-repeat construction (three times), which names an exact count instead of a rate. Paired with rare.

Stative of an event or a kind of event: it occurs at few points over a stretch of time. Own root, not often-NEG, on the more/less precedent (D25 lumps only where the negation really covers the sense; not-often takes in both rare and never). Never is the none determiner before the time root (D62) and is not this root.

The one that comes immediately after in a sequence or in time: the next step, the next run, the next day (tomorrow). Stands before the root it restricts, like the statives. Carved from the after relational word (w0067), which only orders two named things and does not pick out the immediately following member, and from begin (w0103). Verbal use: to follow, to come next. Paired with previous.

The one that comes immediately before in a sequence or in time: the previous version, the previous stage, the previous day (yesterday). Shares its first syllable with next. Not new-NEG (w0112), which is about age, and not the before relational word, which orders two named things. Verbal use: to precede.

One act in an ordered series of acts: a step of a procedure, a move in a process, one instruction carried out. Carved from part (w0055), which is a component of a thing and not an act, and from stage, which is a larger span containing steps. A procedure is not a separate root: step plus the list root (a list of steps) says it. As a verb: to take a step, to carry out one step.

A named span of a process with its own character, containing steps: the setup stage, the run stage, the review stage. Shares its first syllable with step. Carved from step (one act) and from the time root (any point or stretch, with no place in a process). Verbal use: to be at a stage, to be in a phase.

Stative: everything needed is in place, so the thing can begin. Carved from set up (w0078), which is the act of arranging an apparatus: this root is the state arrival at which that act aims, and it holds of people and of things that were never set up by anyone. Not done (w0065), which is the state after finishing, and not able (w0134), which is capacity regardless of preparation. As an argument: readiness.

Halt a running thing with the expectation that it goes on from where it left off; the halt itself. Shares its first syllable with begin and stop, the same family. Carved from stop (w0102), which ends the thing, and from wait (w0054), which is letting time pass, not halting anything. Transitive (pause the run) or intransitive (the machine paused). Paired with continue.

Go on from where a thing stands, without starting over: keep going, or take it up again after a pause. Lumped: carrying on and resuming are one root, since both are the opposite of starting over. Carved from repeat (w0087), which does the whole thing again from the beginning, and from begin (w0103). Paired with pause; same family as begin and stop.

The point in a sequence at which it falls to a given party to act: my turn, your turn, whose turn. Built audibly from the person family. Carved from the repeat root (w0087), which already covers a round, an iteration or a go of a repeated thing: this root is about whose go it is, not about the go itself. The party is the possessor. Verbal use: for it to be someone's turn.

The stretch that lies between two points or two events: the gap between runs, the space between two lines, the wait between a request and its answer. Carved from the time root (w0049), which is a point or stretch taken on its own, and from wait (w0054), which is a person letting time pass. The language has no word for 'between'; a compound (run interval) or the possessor case names the two ends. Verbal use: to lie between.

A unit of work someone takes on and can finish: a job, a ticket, an item of work. Verbal: to work on, to do as one's work. Carved from thing (w0046, any entity) and from the change carve (fix/alter/build name what is done to a thing; this root names the assigned unit of work itself, whatever is done in it). Not the goal (the state aimed at) and not the plan (the ordered whole).

How much work a thing costs: labour, workload, the amount of doing a task demands. Stative/verbal: to cost work, to take effort. Same first syllable as task: this is the size of the task, not the task. Carved from time (w0049, how long it lasts) and from difficulty (how hard it is): a long or hard task and a big-effort task are different claims. Not more/less (w0083-84), which are bare amounts.

An ordered set of intended acts for reaching a goal: a plan, a schedule, an approach. Verbal: to plan, to lay out what will be done. Carved from decide (w0126, settling one open question) and from the intend stance (commitment to one act): a plan is the whole shape of the work, may be made by one party for another, and can exist without commitment. Not the goal, which is its end point.

The state of affairs the work is aimed at: the end wanted, the objective, what done would mean here. Verbal: to aim at, to have as the goal. Carved from result (w0048, what actually comes about, whether wanted or not) and from want (w0137, a person's desire): the goal is the target itself, and work can miss it. Shares its first syllable with plan and priority, the direction family.

Which work is to be done before which: rank in the order of doing. Verbal: to rank, to have priority. Carved from list/order (w0108, sequence of anything) and from big (w0059, importance or size in general): a small task can have high priority. High priority = priority + big; low = priority + small. Not should (w0138), which says a thing ought to be done at all, not when.

How far a piece of work has come toward being done, and the making of that headway. Verbal: to make progress, to move along. Carved from done (w0065, the end state) and from increase (w0085, a value going up): progress is the covered part of a task, it can be reported and compared while nothing is finished. Not the result.

Cannot go on until something else happens; be held up by it. The blocker takes the object case. Verbal and stative. Carved from wait (w0054, letting time pass, which may be idle choice) and from able-NEG (w0134, lacking the capacity): a blocked person is able and not idle, and is stopped by a named other thing. Not stop (w0102), which halts a thing that was running.

The tie between a person and a piece of work that makes it theirs to do and theirs to answer for. The work takes the object case. Lumped on purpose: English responsible, accountable, owner of and whose job it is are one root here, since between two people they never come apart. Not possession (the possessor case, w0017) and not hold/exist (w0064). As an argument: a responsibility, an owner's charge.

Move the responsibility for a piece of work from one person to another. The one giving it up is the subject and the receiver takes the location case; for take over, the receiver is the subject and the former holder takes 'from'. Also covers assigning work that had no holder. Carved from give/pass (w0111), which moves a thing, and from show (w0113): what moves here is the charge, not the object. As an argument: a handover.

Hold or do a thing jointly, or split it between people: share a task, share the data, split the effort. The other party takes 'with'; the thing shared is the object. Carved from give (w0111, which leaves the giver without it), from hand over (the charge passes entirely) and from with (w0023, mere accompaniment): sharing leaves both parties holding it. As an argument: a share, a split.

Tell the person who needs it how the work stands. The content is the object or a bare subordinate clause; the person reported to takes the location case. Carved from say/tell (w0121, any utterance), from show (w0113, making visible) and from explain (w0117, giving an account so it is grasped): reporting is owed, is about the state of work, and needs no explaining. As an argument: a report.

A short written thing left for a person to read later: a memo, a comment in code, a line left on the matter. Verbal: to leave a note. Carved from record (w0088), which captures an observed value into a durable store for the data, and from write (w0043, producing text or code) and message (w0105, output sent by a machine or party): a note is written for a person to come back to.

A matter that is not settled and is kept on a list until it is: an open question, an outstanding point, a to-do that is still a question rather than a task. Verbal: to be open, to remain unsettled. Carved from ask-for-information (w0032, the act of asking), from question particle and from task: nobody need have asked it aloud, and it is closed by deciding, not by doing. Closed = decide, or open-item-NEG.

Stative: with no other person in it; doing or being by oneself. Together is the with construction (w0023) or this root negated, so only one root is coined (D25 pattern). Said of a person, or of an act through the while construction: at the time that I was alone. Carved from the none determiner (w0136) and from help-NEG (w0125): being alone is a state, not a lack of assistance.

Rely on a person to do what they said they would, or on a machine to behave. The person relied on takes the object case; the matter relied on for takes 'with'. Carved from the trust stance (w0008), which is the speaker relying on a proposition as an assumption: this root is a standing relation between two people that can be built, held and lost, and can be the object of other verbs. Not agree (w0115) and not belief (w0028).

A bad outcome that may come, named as a thing: a hazard, an exposure, what could go wrong here. Verbal: to be dangerous. Carved from the risk stance (w0009), which is the speaker flagging that their own claim may go wrong, and from chance (w0092, randomness with no cause): a danger can be found, listed, compared and removed. Not fault (w0030) and not failure (w0031), which are actual.
Seven days taken as one unit. Calendar units share a first syllable with day and night so the set is audible (D85).
A calendar month. Not defined against the week or the day here; a span of roughly thirty days.
A calendar year.
A clock hour. Clock units share the calendar first syllable, since both answer the how-long and when questions.
A clock minute.

Put a thing to work for a purpose: use a function, a machine, a file, a method. The thing used is the object; the purpose takes the for word. Carved against run, which is making something execute, and against take, which is acquiring it. As an argument: a use.

The subject must have or do the thing for something else to hold. Modal-shaped in meaning but a plain root: the thing needed is the object, or a subordinate clause. Carved against want, which is desire, and against should, which is what ought to be done: one can need what one does not want.
One case shown to stand for a kind. What a corpus sentence is to the language. Carved against sample, which is drawn to represent a population for measurement, and against part.
One word of a language, as a unit of meaning; also a term or a name for a kind. Carved against text, which is characters as data, and against name, which identifies one thing.
How big a thing is, as a measurable quantity. The stative big and small say which end; this is the dimension itself, the thing a measurement of bigness yields.

Determiner slot, standing before a numeral or a root exactly where every/all (w0135) and no/none (w0136) stand, and on the same consonant as both. Quantitative approximation only: it hedges an amount or a degree, never a claim. Hedging a claim is the stance slot's job — risk and propose (D34) — and the two must not be confused. With a numeral it is 'about five'; with a stative root it is 'almost done'. A reserve syllable spent by decision (D123).

Basic colour term. The colour family sits on the look root, because a colour is a seen quality; members are told apart by the second syllable's vowel, in the order languages acquire basic colour terms. Covers the focal colour and its whole range; no separate light, dark or saturation terms exist and none should be coined (D123).
Basic colour term, the look family (D123). Focal colour and its range; see the black entry for the family's carve.
